In this activity we return to the dogwood trees from the Vector Data activity. These are 58 maternal trees sampled along a gradient from the city of Richmond, Virginia, south to Pocahontas State Park. Back then, the `get_landcover()` function did the raster work for you because we had not covered rasters yet. Now we have, so this time you will pull the land cover out of the raster yourself and then use a regression to describe how the landscape changes along the gradient.

## The Data

The trees are in the course data repository. `Habitat` is `Urban`, `Suburban`, or `Native`, and `N` is the number of offspring (seeds) collected from each tree. This time we use all 58 trees, not just the `Preliminary` ones.

```{r}
url <- "https://dyerlabteaching.github.io/CourseData/Spatial/Richmond_Dogwoods.csv"
read_csv( url ) |>
  st_as_sf( coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326 ) -> trees
trees
```

The land cover is the 2021 [National Land Cover Database](https://www.mrlc.gov/data) (NLCD) on 30 m cells. Each cell holds a class code; codes `21` through `24` are the four classes of *developed* land (open space, low, medium, and high intensity). See the [NLCD legend](https://www.mrlc.gov/data/legends/national-land-cover-database-class-legend-and-description) for the rest.

```{r}
nlcd <- rast( "https://dyerlabteaching.github.io/CourseData/Spatial/Richmond_NLCD_2021.tif" )
nlcd
```

We will measure distances from Richmond City Hall, in the middle of downtown.

```{r}
data.frame( Name = "City Hall",
            Longitude = -77.4334,
            Latitude = 37.5407 ) |>
  st_as_sf( coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326 ) -> downtown
```

## The Question

4. Define each tree's neighborhood as everything within 500 m (`st_buffer()`), and find the proportion of each neighborhood that is developed. When you `terra::extract()` with polygons rather than points, you get back one row for *every cell* inside each polygon, and the `ID` column says which polygon (tree) that cell belongs to. Keep the `ID` this time (leave off `ID = FALSE`). Then use `group_by()` and `summarize()` to collapse the cells to one value per tree. The mean of a `TRUE`/`FALSE` column is the proportion of `TRUE` cells.
